analysis.one_liner: Forces a full NAFTA review and threatens U.S. withdrawal unless eight conditions are certified.
analysis.headline: The NAFTA Accountability Act gathered 92 cosponsors but never got a hearing or vote in the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the government to measure what NAFTA did to trade, jobs, wages, food safety, drug smuggling, and pollution along the U.S.-Mexico border. If officials could not certify that NAFTA met benchmarks in eight areas by early 1998, the United States would give six months' notice and leave the agreement at the start of 1999. The President would also have to renegotiate NAFTA's terms, and Congress said fast-track authority for expanding NAFTA should be off the table until the conditions were met.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. manufacturing workers facing job losses from plant relocations to Mexico, American farmers and ranchers hit by import surges, small food producers facing imports below U.S. health standards, border communities affected by pollution and disease, and motorists concerned about unsafe Mexican trucks on U.S. roads. It also gave leverage to any member skeptical of expanding NAFTA.

how_it_helps.text: Requires cabinet secretaries to certify in eight areas, including that trade with Mexico and Canada has created more specific U.S. jobs than it has cost and that real hourly wages have not fallen since NAFTA took effect.

Directs the President to renegotiate NAFTA so tariffs and quotas adjust when imports surge, currency swings become severe, food safety degrades, drug flows rise, or import surges hurt U.S. agriculture.

Provides for the U.S. to withdraw from NAFTA by January 1, 1999 unless every certification is met before March 31, 1998, and states that NAFTA should not be expanded and fast-track authority should not be renewed until then.
Orders reports on border-zone pollution, disease rates, contaminated food imports, drug flows, and truck safety inspections, bringing NAFTA's side effects to Congress and the public.

analysis.who_pays: Exporters, importers, and companies that had moved production to Mexico would face the risk of tariffs, quotas, renegotiated terms, or U.S. withdrawal if the certifications failed. Farmers, retailers, and consumers relying on Mexican and Canadian imports could face higher prices or supply disruptions.

drawbacks.text: The bill conditions continued U.S. membership in NAFTA on eight certifications including subjective judgments on 'democracy and human freedoms' in Canada and Mexico, and would have terminated approval if any condition failed by March 31, 1998, with the withdrawal process starting July 1, 1998 — leaving little room for renegotiation to actually fix the problems first.

Currency certification requires exchange rates within 10 percent of NAFTA-era levels, a benchmark the peso crisis had already blown through and that no trading partner could realistically satisfy on that timeline.

Renegotiating tariffs and quotas when imports exceed 10 percent of exports, or when currencies move, risks inviting retaliation and raising prices for U.S. consumers and businesses that rely on North American supply chains.

Withdrawing from a trade agreement could disrupt agriculture, autos, and other sectors that had built cross-border operations, and could strain relations with two of the country's closest trading partners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core value was accountability — forcing a real accounting of NAFTA's effects on jobs, wages, food safety, and the border environment, and giving the U.S. genuine leverage to renegotiate rather than simply accept the status quo. But the design was blunt: the certification deadlines were extremely tight, the benchmarks were hard targets that were almost certain to fail, and the remedy for failure was full withdrawal rather than a graduated renegotiation, which risked serious economic disruption for a goal that might have been achieved with less drastic tools.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Subcommittee on Trade on March 6, 1997, and no further action was ever taken on it in the 105th Congress.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 6, 1997 by Rep. Marcy Kaptur with 45 original cosponsors and referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Subcommittee on Trade.
The bill accumulated 92 cosponsors, including 63 Democrats, 28 Republicans, and 1 Independent, showing substantial bipartisan support in the House.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred; the Ways and Means Committee took no action and the bill died at the end of the 105th Congress in January 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Importers, exporters, and companies that had moved production to Mexico benefited, because the threat of tariffs, renegotiation, or U.S. withdrawal never materialized. Members of Congress who supported free trade also avoided a politically difficult vote on a bill with broad bipartisan backing.

for.name: Rep. Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 45 original cosponsors.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee Chair Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, so the bill never advanced.

against.name: Subcommittee on Trade Chair Phil Crane
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on the bill.

against.name: Clinton administration
against.what_they_did: Supported NAFTA as passed and opposed renegotiation or withdrawal; the bill would have blocked the fast-track authority the administration was seeking.

against.name: Business and trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed efforts to renegotiate or withdraw from NAFTA.

sides.party_line_note: The 92 cosponsors split 63 Democrats, 28 Republicans, and 1 Independent, so support was bipartisan, but there was no recorded vote to measure opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed automatic tariffs and quotas when imports exceeded a threshold relative to exports, and risked full U.S. withdrawal from NAFTA, disrupting cross-border trade.
Facilities and jobs moved to Mexico under NAFTA would have faced the risk of renegotiated terms or withdrawal, undermining the cost advantages of offshoring.
U.S. farmers hurt by import surges from Canada and Mexico would gain renegotiated protections, but the threat of withdrawal could disrupt export markets for U.S. agriculture.
Stricter certification of food safety standards and potential tariffs would raise costs for businesses importing food products from Mexico and Canada.
The bill's job-creation certification and renegotiation mandates were designed to protect and restore U.S. manufacturing employment.
Requirements for comprehensive inspection of Mexican trucks entering the U.S. would raise compliance costs, though the bill aimed to improve highway safety.
